claim: Somatosensory feedback is transmitted to many sensory and motor cortical regions within 25 ms of a mechanical disturbance applied to the monkey's arm.
source: Here we show that somatosensory feedback is transmitted to many sensory and motor cortical regions within 25 ms of a mechanical disturbance applied to the monkey's arm.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by experimental data showing perturbation onset times across cortical areas (A5:21 ms, A2:18 ms, S1:17 ms, M1:22 ms, PMd:25 ms) as shown in Figure 1E and described in the Results section.

claim: When limb feedback was salient to an ongoing motor action (task engagement), neurons in parietal area 5 immediately (~25 ms) increased their response to limb disturbances.
source: When limb feedback was salient to an ongoing motor action (task engagement), neurons in parietal area 5 immediately (~25 ms) increased their response to limb disturbances, whereas neurons in other regions did not alter their response until 15 to 40 ms later.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that A5 population signal was reduced in the Movie vs Posture Task at 23 ms, while other cortical areas showed reduction at ~40 ms or later (M1: 38 ms, PMd: 42 ms, S1: 40 ms and A2: 70 ms).

claim: Neurons in regions other than parietal area 5 did not alter their response to limb disturbances during task engagement until 15 to 40 ms after the initial response.
source: When limb feedback was salient to an ongoing motor action (task engagement), neurons in parietal area 5 immediately (~25 ms) increased their response to limb disturbances, whereas neurons in other regions did not alter their response until 15 to 40 ms later.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing differential signal onset times across cortical areas during task engagement (M1: 38 ms, PMd: 42 ms, S1: 40 ms and A2: 70 ms) as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Initiation of a motor action elicited by a limb disturbance (target selection) altered neural responses in primary motor cortex ~65 ms after the limb disturbance.
source: In contrast, initiation of a motor action elicited by a limb disturbance (target selection) altered neural responses in primary motor cortex ~65 ms after the limb disturbance, and then in dorsal premotor cortex, with no effect in parietal regions until 150 ms post-perturbation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing differences in M1 population signals for IN and OUT targets first observed at 66 ms after perturbation onset (Figure 4B,C).

claim: Target selection altered neural responses in dorsal premotor cortex after changes in primary motor cortex.
source: In contrast, initiation of a motor action elicited by a limb disturbance (target selection) altered neural responses in primary motor cortex ~65 ms after the limb disturbance, and then in dorsal premotor cortex, with no effect in parietal regions until 150 ms post-perturbation.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing PMd differential signal onset at 98 ms, after M1 at 66 ms (Figure 4B,C).

claim: Target selection had no effect on neural responses in parietal regions until 150 ms post-perturbation.
source: In contrast, initiation of a motor action elicited by a limb disturbance (target selection) altered neural responses in primary motor cortex ~65 ms after the limb disturbance, and then in dorsal premotor cortex, with no effect in parietal regions until 150 ms post-perturbation.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing population signals in S1 and A5 did not show any difference across targets until ~150 ms post-perturbation (Figure 4B,C).

claim: Broad parietofrontal circuits provide the neural substrate for goal-directed corrections.
source: Our findings highlight broad parietofrontal circuits that provide the neural substrate for goal-directed corrections, an essential aspect of highly skilled motor behaviors.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental findings showing distributed task-dependent processing across multiple cortical regions (A5, A2, S1, M1, PMd).

claim: Optimal feedback control (OFC) has become an influential theory for interpreting voluntary motor control.
source: Optimal feedback control (OFC) has become an influential theory for interpreting voluntary motor control (Todorov and Jordan, 2002; Scott, 2004; 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on OFC theory.

claim: OFC includes state estimation based on sensory and internally generated feedback.
source: OFC includes state estimation (i.e. position and velocity of the body segments) based on sensory and internally generated feedback.
evidence: The claim draws from established understanding of OFC theory as referenced in the introduction.

claim: OFC includes a control policy that uses state estimates to generate motor commands to muscles that generate movement to attain a behavioral goal.
source: It also includes a control policy that uses these state estimates to generate motor commands to muscles that generate movement to attain a behavioral goal.
evidence: The claim draws from established understanding of OFC theory as referenced in the introduction.

claim: Feedback gains within the control policy are selected based on the behavioral goal.
source: Importantly, feedback gains within the control policy are selected based on the behavioral goal.
evidence: The claim draws from established understanding of OFC theory as referenced in the introduction.

claim: Muscle responses are modified in under 100ms due to behavioral factors such as task instruction.
source: This approach has been used to show how muscle responses are modified in under 100ms due to behavioral factors such as task instruction (Hammond et al., 1956; Rothwell et al., 1980; Pruszynski et al., 2008; Shemmell et al., 2009), the properties of the spatial target and selection of alternate goals (Yang et al., 2011; Nashed et al., 2012; Selen et al., 2012), location of obstacles in the environment (Nashed et al., 2012; 2014), mechanical properties of the limb and environment (Kurtzer et al., 2008; Shemmell et al., 2010; Cluff and Scott, 2013; Weiler et al., 2015), and timing constraints or task urgency (Crevecoeur et al., 2013; Omrani et al., 2013; Cluff and Scott, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies demonstrating task-dependent muscle responses.

claim: The neural basis of task-dependent feedback processing is largely unexplored.
source: The neural basis of this task-dependent feedback processing is, however, largely unexplored.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of the literature and provides motivation for the current study.

claim: Frontoparietal circuits are known to play an important role in voluntary control.
source: Frontoparietal circuits are known to play an important role in voluntary control, but the focus for the last 30 years has been on motor planning and the initiation of motor actions (Kalaska et al., 1997; Andersen and Cui, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on frontoparietal circuits.

claim: The focus on frontoparietal circuits for the last 30 years has been on motor planning and the initiation of motor actions.
source: Frontoparietal circuits are known to play an important role in voluntary control, but the focus for the last 30 years has been on motor planning and the initiation of motor actions (Kalaska et al., 1997; Andersen and Cui, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and represents a historical assessment of the field.

claim: Perturbation-related activity in a brain region that is not influenced by the behavioral goal would be associated with state estimation.
source: From this perspective, perturbation-related activity in a brain region that is not influenced by the behavioral goal would be associated with the former, whereas perturbation-related activity that is modified by the behavioral goal, would be associated with the latter.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the OFC framework and provides a theoretical interpretation framework for the study.

claim: Perturbation-related activity that is modified by the behavioral goal would be associated with the control policy.
source: From this perspective, perturbation-related activity in a brain region that is not influenced by the behavioral goal would be associated with the former, whereas perturbation-related activity that is modified by the behavioral goal, would be associated with the latter.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the OFC framework and provides a theoretical interpretation framework for the study.

claim: Several sensory and motor cortical areas respond to mechanical loads applied to the limb.
source: There are sporadic observations that several sensory and motor cortical areas respond to mechanical loads applied to the limb (Tanji et al., 1980; Chapman et al., 1984; Crammond et al., 1986; Boudreau et al., 2001; Weber and He, 2004; London and Miller, 2012; Spieser et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Task-dependent changes in neural activity have only been examined in primary sensory (S1) and motor cortices (M1).
source: However, task-dependent changes in neural activity have only been examined in primary sensory (S1) and motor cortices (M1) (Evarts and Tanji, 1974; Wolpaw, 1980; Omrani et al., 2014; Pruszynski et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and represents an assessment of the existing literature.

claim: The extent to which other cortical regions are involved in generating task-dependent feedback responses remains largely unexplored.
source: Thus, the extent to which other cortical regions are involved in generating these task-dependent feedback responses (i.e. part of the control policy) remains largely unexplored.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of the literature and provides motivation for the current study.

claim: The activity of 611 neurons was recorded in 5 different cortical regions associated with voluntary motor control.
source: The activity of 611 neurons was recorded in 5 different cortical regions associated with voluntary motor control (A5:posterior parietal area 5, A2:primary somatosensory area 2, S1:primary somatosensory area 1 & 3, M1:primary motor cortex and PMd:dorsal premotor cortex, See Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement of the experimental methods and data collection.

claim: Many neurons in each cortical region displayed significant perturbation-related activity within 100 ms of loads being applied in their preferred torque direction.
source: We found many neurons in each cortical region displayed significant perturbation-related activity within 100 ms of loads being applied in their preferred torque direction (Figure 1D, refer to Table 1 for details on the number of neurons recorded in each area and neurons responsive to perturbations).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Table 1.

claim: The magnitude of the perturbation-related responses varied across cortical regions.
source: Although neurons in each cortical region responded to the applied perturbations, the magnitude of the perturbation-related responses varied across cortical regions (one way ANOVA, p<0.0001, F(df=4, error=439)=10.62, See Table 2 for details).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) of experimental data.

claim: The response in S1 was significantly larger than responses in all other areas.
source: A post-hoc analysis revealed that the response in S1 was significantly larger than responses in all other areas (p<0.001, Tukey's least significant difference (LSD) procedure).
evidence: The claim is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: M1 activity was significantly larger than that of A5 and PMd.
source: M1 activity was also significantly larger than that of A5 and PMd (p=0.002 and 0.0009 respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The perturbation response was not significantly different across A5, A2, and PMd.
source: The perturbation response was not significantly different across other areas (p>0.07 in all other comparisons).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The activity of 22/213 M1 neurons correlated with kinematic changes in the postural perturbation task.
source: We found the activity of 22/213 M1 neurons correlated with kinematic changes in the postural perturbation task (p<0.05 threshold).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: Across the M1 population, the median correlation between neural activity and kinematic changes was -0.11.
source: Across the M1 population, the median correlation was -0.11 (p=0.002 in comparison with 0 using a Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Perturbation-related activity in cortical regions other than M1 was not significantly correlated with motor corrections.
source: Perturbation-related activity in the other cortical regions was not significantly correlated with motor corrections although the data samples were smaller than that for M1 (median correlation coefficient, A5: -0.014, A2: -0.001, S1: -0.11, PMd: 0.03, p>0.35 in all areas in comparison with 0 using a Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Perturbation-related activity arrived quickly in all cortical regions with onset times ranging from 17-25 ms.
source: Perturbation onset time for each cortical area was calculated based on the time point when the population signal crossed 3SD above baseline activity (and remained above for at least 20 ms), highlighting that perturbation-related activity arrived quickly in all cortical regions (onset time, A5:21 ms, A2:18 ms, S1:17 ms, M1:22 ms, PMd:25 ms).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of population signals shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Using a running t-test technique, response onset times were generally similar to those observed using the 3SD technique.
source: Response onset times, using this technique were generally similar to those observed using the 3SD technique (A5:25 ms, A2:25 ms, S1:19 ms, M1:24 ms, PMd:34 ms).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of two different analysis methods on the same experimental data.

claim: Sensory feedback from the limb is rapidly transmitted throughout sensory and motor cortical regions.
source: Thus, sensory feedback from the limb is rapidly transmitted throughout sensory and motor cortical regions.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on perturbation onset times across cortical areas.

claim: Primary somatosensory cortex was the first to respond to perturbations, ranking 1st 95% of the time in bootstrap analysis.
source: This analysis revealed that primary somatosensory cortex was the first to respond (with S1 and A2 ranking 1st 95% of the time-S1:77% & A2:18%), premotor cortex was the last to respond (ranking last, 92%), and A5 and M1 responded in between these extremes.
evidence: The claim is supported by bootstrap analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Premotor cortex was the last to respond to perturbations, ranking last 92% of the time in bootstrap analysis.
source: This analysis revealed that primary somatosensory cortex was the first to respond (with S1 and A2 ranking 1st 95% of the time-S1:77% & A2:18%), premotor cortex was the last to respond (ranking last, 92%), and A5 and M1 responded in between these extremes.
evidence: The claim is supported by bootstrap analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Hand and joint motions were similar across Posture and Movie tasks for the first 100 ms.
source: Hand and joint motions were similar across tasks for the first 100 ms.
evidence: The claim is based on kinematic analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Corrective movements and long-latency muscle stretch responses in the Movie Task were greatly diminished as compared to the Posture Task.
source: Importantly, corrective movements, and corresponding long-latency muscle stretch responses in the Movie Task, were greatly diminished as compared to the Posture Task (average muscle response to the perturbation started 34 ms post-perturbation and differentiated across tasks 45 ms post-perturbation, Omrani et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citation to a previous study.

claim: Activity of 416 neurons was recorded in the Posture and Movie Tasks, with 305 displaying significant perturbation responses in the Posture Task.
source: Activity of 416 neurons was recorded in the Posture and Movie Tasks, with 305 displaying significant perturbation responses in the Posture Task (refer to Table 1 for details on the number of neurons responsive to perturbation in each area).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement of the experimental data collection.

claim: Perturbation-related activity was commonly modulated between the Posture and Movie Tasks.
source: Perturbation-related activity was commonly modulated between the Posture and Movie Tasks (Figure 3A, refer to Table 1 for details on the number of neurons).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Table 1.

claim: In most cases, the perturbation response was smaller in the Movie Task than in the Posture Task.
source: In most cases, the response was smaller in the Movie Task (refer to Table 1 for details on the number of neurons).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data summarized in Table 1.

claim: The magnitude of the perturbation response was significantly different across tasks and areas.
source: The magnitude of the perturbation response was significantly different across tasks and areas (mixed ANOVA with task as within-subject and area as between-subject variables, p<0.0001, F(1,300)=62.7 for the task effect and p=0.04, F(4,300)=2.5 for the interaction of task and area).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (mixed ANOVA) of experimental data.

claim: The magnitude of the reduction in perturbation response was significant in A5, M1 and PMd.
source: The magnitude of the reduction was significant in A5, M1 and PMd (p<0.01, one sample t-test), and marginally not significant in S1 and A2 (p=0.086 & 0.052 respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Decreases in activity across tasks were only significant in A5, M1 and PMd.
source: Decreases in activity across tasks were only significant in A5, M1 and PMd (one sample t-test, p<0.0001 in A5 and M1, p=0.0016 in PMd and p=0.052 & 0.086 in A2 and S1 respectively, refer to Table 2 for details on the differential activity in each area across tasks).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: M1 differential response was significantly bigger than the differential response in A2 and PMd.
source: A post-hoc analysis (LSD) revealed that M1 differential response was significantly bigger than the differential response in A2 (p=0.009) and PMd (p=0.03).
evidence: The claim is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The relative change in the perturbation response was significantly different across areas.
source: We also quantified the relative change in the perturbation response in each area (i.e. evoked response in the Posture minus that in the Movie tasks, divided by the evoked response in the Posture Task, refer to Table 2 for details on the relative change in each area across tasks) and found it to be significantly different across areas (One way ANOVA with area as fixed variable and cells as random variables, p=0.019, F(4,300)=3).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) of experimental data.

claim: The relative changes in the perturbation response were significantly smaller in S1 and A2 than in A5, M1, and PMd.
source: A post-hoc analysis (LSD) revealed that the relative changes in the perturbation response were significantly smaller in S1 and A2 than the change ratio in other areas (relative to A2, A5:p=0.036, M1:0.024 and PMd:0.016, and relative to S1, A5: p=0.025, M1:0.019, PMd:0.012).
evidence: The claim is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The change ratio was not significantly different between A5, M1 and PMd.
source: The change ratio was not significantly different between A5, M1 and PMd (relative to A5, M1:p=0.95, PMd:0.65, also p=0.57 in M1-PMd comparison) or between A2 and S1 (p=0.64).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The timing of the change in the perturbation response varied across the cortical areas.
source: Of particular importance is that the timing of the change in the perturbation response varied across the cortical areas.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing different onset times for task-dependent changes across cortical areas.

claim: The population signal for A5 was reduced in the Movie as compared to the Posture Task at 23 ms.
source: The population signal for A5 was reduced in the Movie as compared to the Posture Task at 23 ms, effectively at the same time as the onset of the initial perturbation response in this cortical region (Figure 3B,C, differential signal >3SD of baseline).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Other cortical areas only displayed a significant reduction in the population signal at ~40 ms or later after the applied load.
source: In contrast, other cortical areas only displayed a significant reduction in the population signal at ~40 ms or later after the applied load (M1: 38 ms, PMd: 42 ms, S1: 40 ms and A2: 70 ms).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on differential signal onset times.

claim: Using the running t-test, response differentiation times were 25 ms, 45 ms and 52 ms for A5, M1 and PMd, respectively.
source: Response differentiation times were 25 ms, 45 ms and 52 ms for A5, M1 and PMd, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data using the running t-test method.

claim: Bootstrap analysis identified the most likely order of response differentiation to be A5 first (ranking 1st 89%), then M1, PMd, S1 and last A2 (ranking last 73%).
source: Finally, our bootstrap analysis identified the most likely order of response differentiation to be A5 (ranking 1st 89%, all other regions each less than 5%, middle panel Figure 2A), then M1, PMd, S1 and last A2 (ranking last 73%).
evidence: The claim is supported by bootstrap analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Loads in the target selection task either pushed the hand into the spatial target (IN) or away from it (OUT), eliciting a larger corrective response in the latter condition.
source: Loads in this target selection task either pushed the hand into the spatial target (IN) or away from it (OUT), eliciting a larger corrective response in the latter condition(Figure 1C, Pruszynski et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental design and citation to a previous study.

claim: Differences in muscle responses between the IN and OUT targets begin ~85 ms after the applied load.
source: Differences in muscle responses between the IN and OUT targets begin ~85 ms after the applied load (See Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by EMG data analysis described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Activity of 263 neurons was recorded in the IN and OUT tasks; with 215 displaying significant perturbation responses in the OUT target Task.
source: Activity of 263 neurons was recorded in the IN and OUT tasks; with 215 displaying significant perturbation responses in the OUT target Task (refer to Table 1 for details on the number of neurons responsive to perturbation in each area).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement of the experimental data collection.

claim: Perturbation responses in M1 and PMd were commonly altered between the IN and OUT targets.
source: Perturbation responses in M1 and PMd were commonly altered between the IN and OUT targets (Figure 4, refer to Table 1 for details on the number of neurons).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: Altered responses were also observed in A5, but rarely in somatosensory cortex.
source: Altered responses were also observed in A5, but rarely in somatosensory cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data summarized in Table 1.

claim: Significant increases in activity in the OUT target were predominantly observed in M1, but not in A5 and PMd.
source: Significant increases in activity in the OUT target were predominantly observed in M1, but not in A5 and PMd (refer to Table 1 for details on the number of neurons).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data summarized in Table 1.

claim: The perturbation magnitude was not significantly different across targets but was significantly different across areas.
source: The perturbation magnitude was not significantly different across targets but was significantly different across areas (mixed ANOVA with target as within-subject and area as between-subject variables, p=0.2, F(1,211)=1.64 for the target effect and p=0.005, F(4,211)=3.85 for the interaction of target and area).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (mixed ANOVA) of experimental data.

claim: M1 was the only area which had a significant difference in its activity across the two targets in the 50–100 ms period.
source: M1 was the only area, which had a significant difference in its activity across the two targets in the 50–100 ms period (one sample t-test, p=0.0001 in M1, p=0.08 in PMd and p>0.3 in A5, A2 and S1, refer to Table 2 for details on the differential activity in each area across tasks).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: M1 differential response between IN and OUT targets was significantly larger than in A5, A2 and S1 but not different than that of PMd.
source: A post-hoc analysis (LSD) revealed that M1 differential response between IN and OUT targets was significantly larger than in A5 (p=0.005), A2 (p=0.004) and S1 (p=0.017) but not different than that of PMd (p=0.08).
evidence: The claim is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The absolute change in magnitude was significantly different across areas.
source: The absolute change in magnitude was significantly different across areas (One way ANOVA, p<0.001, F(4,211)=5.92).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) of experimental data.

claim: The absolute change in activity in M1 was significantly larger than in A5, A2 and S1 but not different than in PMd.
source: A post-hoc analysis (LSD) revealed that the absolute change in activity in M1 was significantly larger than in A5 (p<0.001), A2 (p=0.004) and S1 (p=0.002) but not different than in PMd (p=0.13).
evidence: The claim is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The absolute change in activity was bigger in PMd compared to A5 and S1.
source: The absolute change in activity was also bigger in PMd compared to the absolute change in A5 (p=0.016) and S1 (p=0.04).
evidence: The claim is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The distribution of change in activity was significantly different in M1 compared to A5, A2, S1, and in PMd compared to A5.
source: A two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test revealed that the distribution was significantly different in M1 compared to A5 (p<0.001), A2 (p=0.001), S1 (p=0.004), and in PMd compared to A5 (p=0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) of experimental data.

claim: Differences in the population signals for the IN and OUT targets were first observed in M1, 66 ms after perturbation onset.
source: Differences in the population signals for the IN and OUT targets were first observed in M1, 66 ms after perturbation onset, and then in PMd at 98 ms (Figure 4B,C, differential signal >3SD of baseline).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Differences in the population signals for the IN and OUT targets were observed in PMd at 98 ms.
source: Differences in the population signals for the IN and OUT targets were first observed in M1, 66 ms after perturbation onset, and then in PMd at 98 ms (Figure 4B,C, differential signal >3SD of baseline).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Population signals in S1 and A5 did not show any difference across targets until ~150 ms post-perturbation.
source: In contrast, population signals in S1 and A5 did not show any difference across targets until ~150 ms post-perturbation, and the differential signal in A2 never passed threshold in this task.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on differential signal onset times.

claim: The differential signal in A2 never passed threshold in the IN/OUT task.
source: In contrast, population signals in S1 and A5 did not show any difference across targets until ~150 ms post-perturbation, and the differential signal in A2 never passed threshold in this task.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on differential signal onset times.

claim: Using the running t-test technique, response differentiation times were 72 ms, 180 ms and 160 ms for M1, PMd and A5 respectively.
source: With this technique, response differentiation times were 72 ms, 180 ms and 160 ms for M1, PMd and A5 respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data using the running t-test method.

claim: Bootstrap analysis identified the most likely order of response differentiation to be M1 first (86%), PMd second (58%), followed by S1 and A5 (similar ratio of 35%) and finally A2 (55%).
source: Finally, the bootstrap technique identified the most likely order of response differentiation to be M1 first (86%, all others regions each less than 5%, except for A2 which was 8%, right panel in Figure 2A), PMd second (58%), followed by S1 and A5 (similar ratio of 35%) and finally A2 (55%).
evidence: The claim is supported by bootstrap analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: When the monkey is not rewarded for responding to the mechanical load, limb feedback is rapidly transmitted across the cortex with the greatest and earliest activity in S1 quickly followed by responses in adjacent cortical regions.
source: The top panel highlights perturbation responses when the monkey is not rewarded for responding to the mechanical load, termed the 'default response'. In this case, limb feedback is rapidly transmitted across the cortex with the greatest and earliest activity in S1 quickly followed by responses in adjacent cortical regions.
evidence: The claim is a summary of experimental findings shown in Figure 5 and described in the Results section.

claim: During task engagement, the perturbation response increases immediately in A5 and then in motor cortical regions with minimal effect in primary somatosensory cortex.
source: The middle panel displays how the perturbation response changes between the Movie and Posture Tasks, termed 'task engagement'. In this case, the perturbation response increases immediately in A5 and then in motor cortical regions with minimal effect in primary somatosensory cortex.
evidence: The claim is a summary of experimental findings shown in Figure 5 and described in the Results section.

claim: During target selection, perturbation-responses first increase in M1, and then PMd, with minimal effect in sensory areas until 150 ms.
source: Finally, the bottom panel displays how perturbation responses are altered when they cue the generation of a goal-directed movement, termed 'target selection'. In this case, perturbation-responses first increase in M1, and then PMd, with minimal effect in sensory areas until 150 ms.
evidence: The claim is a summary of experimental findings shown in Figure 5 and described in the Results section.

claim: The prevailing view 30 years ago was that task-dependent changes in long-latency motor responses were provided by a transcortical feedback pathway from primary somatosensory to primary motor cortex.
source: At that time, the prevailing view was that task-dependent changes in long-latency motor responses, that occur 50 to 100 ms after a mechanical disturbance, were provided by a transcortical feedback pathway from primary somatosensory to primary motor cortex (Desmedt, 1977; Brooks, 1986).
evidence: The claim is a historical statement supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The timing of mechanical responses in M1 are sufficiently fast to generate long-latency responses.
source: The timing of mechanical responses in M1 are sufficiently fast to generate these long-latency responses.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and established knowledge about motor response timing.

claim: Evarts and Tanji illustrated that perturbation responses in M1 could be modulated when the disturbance was the cue for the monkey to push or pull a lever.
source: Classic work by Evarts and Tanji illustrated that perturbation responses in M1 could be modulated when the disturbance was the cue for the monkey to push or pull a lever (Evarts and Tanji, 1974).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Further studies implicated the dentate nucleus in task-dependent feedback processing.
source: Further studies implicated the dentate nucleus in this task-dependent feedback processing (Meyer-Lohmann et al., 1975; Vilis et al., 1976; Strick, 1983; Hore and Vilis, 1984), likely through its connections to M1 (Orioli and Strick, 1989; Dum and Strick, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: It has been generally assumed that there was minimal overlap in cortical circuits involved in online feedback processing from the limb (S1 and M1), and the broad parietal and frontal cortical circuits involved in motor planning and initiation.
source: Based on this evidence, it has been generally assumed that there was minimal overlap in cortical circuits involved in online feedback processing from the limb (S1 and M1), and the broad parietal and frontal cortical circuits involved in motor planning and initiation.
evidence: The claim represents a historical assumption in the field based on previous evidence.

claim: The present study provides the first examination of the relative timing and magnitude of perturbation-related activity across sensory and motor cortices in non-human primates.
source: The present study provides the first examination of the relative timing and magnitude of perturbation-related activity across sensory and motor cortices in non-human primates.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the novelty of the current study based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: Even when the animal is not engaged in a limb motor task, limb afferent feedback is still rapidly transmitted to many sensory and motor cortical regions, beginning in S1 and then spreading to adjacent cortical regions.
source: Here we show that even when the animal is not engaged in a limb motor task, limb afferent feedback is still rapidly transmitted to many sensory and motor cortical regions, beginning in S1 and then spreading to adjacent cortical regions (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is a summary of experimental findings shown in Figure 5.

claim: The magnitude of the perturbation response is greatest in S1 and diminishes spatially across the cortex.

source: M1 was the first cortical region to display changes in perturbation-related activity when the applied load was used to initiate movements to the OUT versus the IN target, and occurred prior to changes in proximal limb muscle activity.
